cheribsd-revocation.oracle: MEASURED 2026-10-09, results/2026-10-09-cheribsd/: **NO FAULT, AND NO REUSE.** The sequence completes with aliased=0: the stale pointer was followed, but the chunk it names was never handed to another allocation, because CheriBSD's libc holds a released chunk in QUARANTINE until the revoker has swept every capability to it. So the access reads only the dead object -- the exploitable half of a use-after-free, reading or writing SOMEONE ELSE'S object, did not happen. It is not a fault, because nothing forced a sweep between the free and the access: the stale capability still carried its tag, as the case was built to leave it. revocation control in the same boot: revocation=1 tag_after_sweep=0 reissued=1, then SIGPROT si_code 2 at the control's own probe, so the revoker demonstrably acts in this guest and a completion here is the mechanism's design, not an inactive mechanism. CONTRAST, measured in the sibling nested corpora: there the inner allocator reissues the storage at once and the stale pointer DOES read another object, because nothing reaches free(). Predicted before the run; the prediction held.
cheribsd-revocation.platform: stock CheriBSD purecap, kernel CHERI-PURECAP-QEMU, revocation ON (--runtime-revocation on); cheribsd-abi, cheribsd-bounds and the revocation control all PASSED in the same boot.

native-detect.oracle: the buggy arm's stale pointer reads storage that now belongs to a different live object, and the case's aliasing flag is set; under the fix the pointer is cleared, copied or never followed, so nothing aliases. The arms differ by the upstream fix, not by protection. ASan reports heap-use-after-free at the labelled probe on the buggy arm and is silent on the fixed arm -- keyed on heap-use-after-free, never on the string AddressSanitizer, which LeakSanitizer's summary also matches.

title: a value was released up front and then released again by the function it delegates to
object: the string field value, a g_strdup or g_malloc
lifetime_ender: string_fvalue_free(fv), whose body is g_free(fv->value.string) and which does not clear it
shape: a release performed by both a function and the one it delegates to
allocator_layer: the platform allocator itself: one direct g_malloc-family allocation, no wmem layer. GLib's g_malloc is malloc plus abort-on-failure.
fidelity: model consumer, real lifetime: the allocation, the free and the later access through the stale pointer are upstream's, quoted in PROVENANCE.md. The later access is the same helper called again from val_from_string, the delegate.
status: built 2026-10-08; native arms measured by runners/run-native.sh in the same commit. The platform arms are declared predictions. CheriBSD measured 2026-10-09 (results/2026-10-09-cheribsd/): NOT-REISSUED.
live_proof: absent at the pin: the entry point was renamed -- v4.6.8:epan/ftypes/ftype-string.c has `val_from_literal`, whose body is `return val_from_string(fv, s, 0, err_msg);` with NO preceding string_fvalue_free, so the defective up-front release has 0 occurrences inside it. A bare grep for `string_fvalue_free` counts 10 in the file and does not discriminate. A fix-reversal.
nested_why: the object came straight from g_malloc / g_new / g_new0 / g_strdup / getline -- which on the platform is malloc -- with no wmem allocator between it and the request. So under this inventory's axis, WHO ALLOCATED THE OBJECT, this row is NOT nested. Its sibling ../wmem-repros holds the nested ones.
distinguishing: the second release is in the DELEGATE, so neither function is wrong on its own -- val_from_unparsed clears the old value defensively and val_from_string clears it because it is about to assign. The fix moves the first release into the branch that does not delegate, which is why it is a restructuring rather than a null assignment.
